turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. Can we just do this? I'm shattered, and that waiting room's boiling.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mrs Shah, in you come. Sorry, I had that the wrong way round — sit yourself down.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, doctor. I'm Priya, I live with Mum. She was going to cancel.
[SEG0004] person_1 (PATIENT): I wasn't. Stop talking for me.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Noted. This is your routine blood pressure and cholesterol review. How've you been, in your own words?
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been exhausted since the winter, and dizzy on the stairs. I've watched her grab the rail.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Exhausted, yes. Dizzy, no. I grab the rail because I'm tired, not because the room's spinning. She's dramatising.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right, so the tiredness you both see, the dizziness you don't. When you say since the winter — which winter?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Last winter, or the one before. I can't separate them. It just is.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): I won't pin a date on it, then. Anything in the chest — pain, or getting breathless on the flat?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I'm not breathless. I just want to be left alone, honestly.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Tablets next. Still on the ramipril and the atorvastatin?
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I do her box. Ramipril every morning, and she packed in the cholesterol one.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Not every morning. Every other day. Don't tell him I take it daily when I don't.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay. So ramipril, what strength, and you're clear it's every other day?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Five milligrams. Every other day. It's the blood pressure one. I was told once a day, I know, um, I just don't.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): You were told five milligrams once each morning, by mouth. I'm not cross, I'm only sorting out what goes in. Any cough from it, or ankles puffing up?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No cough. Ankles are normal. I read about the cough and spaced it, and then I just carried on.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the atorvastatin — the cholesterol tablet — stopped completely?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Stopped. I read something online, muscles packing up, the liver, all that, and I thought I'm not chancing it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you stop?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Since Diwali or after. Could've been before. I haven't a clue, so don't keep asking for a date.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The strip was in the cupboard over Diwali. After that I stopped finding it.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): You remember the mithai, not my tablets. I don't know. Leave it.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the date open. What dose were you on?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): Twenty. At night. I'd been swallowing it for years, for the cholesterol. I'm not going back on it today, so don't start.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): I won't start it today. Did that article match anything you actually felt — muscle pains, dark urine?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Legs are fine. Bit achy on the stairs, but I'm sixty-eight, that's not a tablet.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): So nothing you'd call a statin side effect, just the reading. Let me think this through out loud. Pressure on half the ramipril might still look decent, but with no recent cholesterol I'm guessing on that side.
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Also, her husband keeps his diabetes pills in the same drawer. Metformin. I didn't want the lists getting mixed.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): They're his. I don't take them. He's diabetic, I'm not. Can everyone stop mixing us up?
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformin stays off your list entirely. And no one's told you that you have diabetes?
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll take a pressure while we talk. Arm out for me... one hundred and thirty-six over eighty-two. Pulse is seventy-four, nice and steady.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): There. So every other day is fine.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): One clinic reading isn't the whole picture, that's what I'm turning over. Ramipril isn't only today's number, it does a bit for the heart and the kidneys as well. I'd rather five milligrams every morning. I'm not going to pretend you'll do that if you won't.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): I won't. Not this month. I'm too tired to faff with a new routine.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can change the box. I do the mornings anyway, I live there.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): You can change the box all you like. I'm still taking it every other day.

[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we record what you'll actually swallow. Five milligrams every other day, and you tell me if that changes. For bloods, I'm requesting a lipid profile, and kidney function with the electrolytes, because of the ramipril. No sense deciding a statin with no numbers.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): More bloods. Course.

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's one form. I'll send it through, phlebotomy here or your own practice, whichever is less of a trek. If the cholesterol's up, we talk about atorvastatin or something else. If it isn't, we might leave it — I genuinely don't know which yet.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): And if it's up and I still say no?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we have a proper conversation, not a telling-off. I'd like you back in a month either way, results in hand, and we'll revisit the statin then.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't forget, I postpone. And this chair's making my back ache — that's the chair, not me, before anyone writes it down.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): I won't write the chair down. Allergies, anything for the form?
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm aware of.
[SEG0048] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Her mum always said penicillin. A rash, when Mum was small.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): I've had penicillin. Tooth infection, a few years back, nothing happened. So no, I'm not allergic. That was Gran fussing.

[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then I'll put no known allergy that you stand by. I won't list penicillin as fact when you've taken it since and been fine. So, lipids and U and Es on that form, ramipril exactly as you're taking it, none of your husband's metformin, and I'll see you in a month to settle the statin.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): A month. Fine. Are we done?
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): We're done. Go and get a cup of tea, the pair of you.

spec.situation: Patient on routine review who admits stopping the cholesterol tablet after reading something online, still takes the BP tablet but 'every other day'; mentions husband's diabetes pills; doctor does not scold, plans repeat blood tests and revisits the statin decision in a month.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: Patient reports legs a bit achy on stairs; severity 'mild' not explicitly stated.
bad.text: Leg ache (category=musculoskeletal, status=present, severity=mild, temporality=current, body_site=legs, aggravating_factors=climbing stairs, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Patient denies statin side effects generally, but never explicitly denies dark urine.
Dispute is described, but doctor resolves by recording no known allergy, so not unresolved.
bad.text: The caregiver recalls a childhood penicillin rash while the patient denies a penicillin allergy and says she later took penicillin without a reaction. (type=allergy_disputed, related_entities=allergies[0]; negative_findings[6], resolution_status=unresolved)

omissions.text: Dizziness is recorded as present, but the patient explicitly denied dizziness: she said she grabs the rail because she is tired, not because the room is spinning.

Atorvastatin discontinuation was planned to be revisited: if cholesterol is high they will discuss atorvastatin or an alternative, and if not it may be left; the doctor said he did not yet know which way it would go.
The follow-up plan specified returning in one month with the blood test results in hand to revisit and settle the statin decision.
The patient stated she is not going back on atorvastatin today, and later said that if cholesterol is up she may still refuse; this resistance to restarting statin therapy is not captured.

The doctor documented that penicillin should not be listed as an allergy because the patient had taken it for a tooth infection a few years ago without any reaction, and would record no known allergy that the patient stands by. The recorded allergy entry for penicillin as disputed is therefore misleading.

omissions.text: Atorvastatin was stopped because the patient read online about possible muscle and liver problems and chose not to risk it, despite not having experienced those side effects.
Negative finding omitted: the patient denied muscle pains/statin side effects, saying her legs were fine apart from age-related achiness on stairs.

The doctor advised that ramipril had originally been prescribed as 5 mg by mouth once each morning and said he would prefer 5 mg every morning rather than every other day, but accepted recording what the patient will actually take.
The patient explicitly refused to change ramipril to daily dosing at present ('I won't. Not this month').
Phlebotomy location options were discussed: blood tests could be done here or at the patient's own practice, whichever was easier.

Recorded allergy is wrong: penicillin should not be listed as an allergy; the patient said she had taken penicillin for a tooth infection a few years ago without reaction, and the doctor documented no known allergy.
